# Advanced Context Infrastructure (ACI)

> **"The AI doesn't forget. The AI doesn't hallucinate about what happened. The AI maintains itself."**

**Give any AI assistant a persistent, self-maintaining, self-auditing memory — using nothing but markdown files on your machine.** No daemon, no API keys, no cloud service, no vendor. Born from **40+ production sessions** running complex global operations with AI as a true partner, not a one-off chat.

## 2-Minute Start

```bash
# 1. From this repository, copy the starter file
cp templates/level-1-single-file.md my-context.md

# 2. Fill in the sections (who you are, priorities, key people) — 10 minutes

# 3. Every AI session, start with:
#      "Read my-context.md before we begin."
#    End every session with:
#      "Update my-context.md with what changed today."
```

That's the whole loop. Your AI now remembers. Everything else in this repo — the multi-file architecture, the self-correction audits, the structural tooling — is what to add **when you feel specific pain**, and each addition tells you which pain it fixes.

**Works with anything that reads and writes local files:** coding agents, desktop assistants with filesystem access, AI-enabled editors, and MCP-compatible tools. Switching assistants costs nothing—the memory never lived inside the assistant.

---

## Provenance and privacy

This repository ships **generic architecture, templates, and synthetic examples—not a production vault**. Personal content, private implementation details, source identifiers, credentials, and raw records do not belong in a release. Copy the structure into a local workspace, keep canon local, and add only context you are authorized to maintain.

Repository hosting is deployment-specific. This release intentionally makes no claim about an external canonical account or mirror; use the copy and release provenance approved for your environment.

---

## Why files? (vs. context-sync services and memory APIs)

A category of tools now exists to make agent context portable: sync daemons, cloud context stores, session-capture APIs, memory layers. They solve portability by **centralizing raw context in infrastructure**. ACI solves it with **curated files and zero infrastructure**. The difference is not cosmetic:

| | Context-sync / memory services | ACI (file-based vault) |
|---|---|---|
| What's stored | Raw session transcripts, auto-captured | Curated, verified knowledge |
| Quality control | None — capture is the product | Session ritual + Tenth Man audit + structural tooling — **curation is the product** |
| Trust required | Cloud provider, API keys, daemon uptime | None — local markdown |
| Sensitive work | Context leaves your machine | Never leaves your machine |
| Agent lock-in | SDK/API integration per agent | Anything that reads files |
| Cost | Subscription/usage | Zero |

The deeper issue is quality: **automatically accumulated context is unaudited context.** An agent drawing on a growing pile of raw transcripts inherits every error in the pile. An agent drawing on a curated vault inherits verified truth — because everything in it passed through a ritual before becoming "memory." Accumulation is cheap. Curation is the moat.

**We scanned the whole field before making claims** — memory APIs (Letta, Zep, Mem0, cognee), sync services, governed-memory tools (Engram, Bilinc), and the other file-based approaches (Cline Memory Bank, CLAUDE.md, Basic Memory) — including where each is honestly ahead of us and what we adopted in response. → [`COMPARISON.md`](COMPARISON.md)

**And one deliberate contrarian stance:** every memory product optimizes token efficiency; ACI optimizes **correctness**. Verification is a first-class spend — second-pass audits on high-stakes outputs, deterministic provenance/contradiction/staleness checks, a production defect log instead of a retrieval benchmark. → [`guides/quality-ceiling.md`](guides/quality-ceiling.md)

**New in v3:** ACI adds an optional **Control Panel** for safe proactive collection: scheduled read-only scouts create immutable packets, a local synthesizer creates a sealed brief, and any live refresh is bounded and visibly separate. The canonical vault remains local, and no scheduled workflow writes to the vault or an external system. See [The v3 Control Panel](#the-v3-control-panel) below.

The v2 organizing principle remains foundational: **know which parts of your system are deterministic and which are probabilistic, and label them.** Content is passive; rules and agents fire against it; every rule has a tier; failures get hardened down the ladder. See [The D/P Principle](#the-dp-principle-v2) below.

---

## The Problem

- AI sessions start from zero every time
- Context gets lost between sessions
- Facts go stale without anyone noticing
- Contradictions accumulate silently
- Rules you wrote down quietly stop being followed (**drift** — the failure mode nobody talks about)
- The more complex your work, the worse all of it gets

---

## The Solution: Three-Level Architecture

### Level 1: Single File (Start Here)

One markdown file. Everything in one place. Works for simple use cases (1–3 active projects, few stakeholders).

**When to use:** You're just getting started, or your work is focused on a single domain with limited moving parts.

### Level 2: Multi-File (Growing Complexity)

4–7 specialized files. Each answers a different question. Cross-referenced. Works for moderate complexity (5–10 active projects, multiple stakeholders, recurring meetings).

**When to use:** Your single file is getting unwieldy (500+ lines), you're losing things, or you need to separate "who" from "what" from "how."

### Level 3: Relational Architecture (Full Scale)

Core files (always loaded) + Operational Index (router) + Entity Files (on-demand) + Document Registry (intake) + Action Tracker (canonical open-items list). Three-tier memory (Active → Seeds → Deep). Self-correcting (Tenth Man + Kaizen). Structurally audited (Vault Map). Works for high complexity (10+ projects, large teams, multiple domains, strategic + operational work simultaneously).

**When to use:** You're managing across domains, your Level 2 files are bloating, and you need the AI to be selective about what it loads.

---

## The D/P Principle (v2)

The maturity leap in this framework isn't more files — it's **explicitly separating deterministic from probabilistic behavior** across everything that runs.

**Your vault's content files are passive repositories.** They don't fire anything. Rules, actions, and agents fire *against* them — and every one of those belongs to one of three tiers:

| Tier | What it is | Failure mode | Fix class |
|------|-----------|--------------|-----------|
| **D — Deterministic** | Code: scripts, queries, pollers, thresholds | Bugs | Patch once, fixed forever |
| **DP — Deterministic spec, Probabilistic executor** | A hard rule in prose, executed by an LLM | **Silent drift** | Tighten the spec, add a verify step, or harden to D |
| **P — Probabilistic** | Judgment, synthesis, drafting, scoring | "Almost right" | Calibrate, and always review |

The **DP tier is where most of your rules live and most of your failures happen** — the rule stays written down while adherence quietly erodes. The framework's answer is the **hardening ladder**: when a probabilistic behavior fails twice, harden it one tier down. Push mechanical work into code; keep judgment at the top. Probabilistic interprets; deterministic executes and verifies.

**→ Full guide: [`guides/deterministic-vs-probabilistic.md`](guides/deterministic-vs-probabilistic.md)** — the three tiers, the hardening ladder, real production failure stories, and how to tag every rule in your quality contract.

---

## The v3 Control Panel

The **ACI Control Panel** is an optional orchestration layer above a working local vault. It closes the gap between manual session startup and proactive, scheduled preparation without turning a cloud service into a second memory system.

```text
scheduled triggers → orchestrator → cloud/local agent runtime
→ narrow read-only source skills → immutable packets
→ local canonical-vault synthesizer → sealed brief → bounded live delta
```

The trust boundaries are the feature:

- **Least privilege and source allowlists:** each scout reads one named source slice through one narrow skill.
- **Packets, not capture exhaust:** normalized facts only—no raw transcripts, full source dumps, credentials, source identifiers, or entire-vault copies.
- **Local canon:** cloud runtimes never receive the whole vault; synthesis happens locally against routed files.
- **No autonomous writes:** scheduled agents cannot modify the vault or an external system. A local canonical writer acts only on a human-approved exact diff and reads the result back.
- **Honest output health:** every packet and brief is `READY`, `DEGRADED`, or `BLOCKED`; unavailable values carry an explicit reason.
- **Operational safety:** end-to-end idempotency, bounded transient retries, content-free observability, staged rollout, and a tested rollback path.
- **No self-modifying governance:** an operational agent cannot modify the deterministic mechanism, tests, baseline, schema, or acceptance criteria governing its own run; changes use a separate human-approved maintenance workflow.
- **Sealed means sealed:** optional live delta is human-initiated, allowlisted, time/call/record bounded, and cannot alter the brief or vault.

Financial-health outputs always render **YTD through the prior closed month**, **prior-month close**, and **MTD or an explicit unavailable state**.

Start with [`guides/control-panel.md`](guides/control-panel.md) or the plain-language [`guides/control-panel-checklist.md`](guides/control-panel-checklist.md). The Control Panel is optional; Levels 1–3 continue to work with files alone.

---

## Key Concepts

### Memory Tiers

| Tier | Description | Loaded At Start? | Update Frequency |
|------|-------------|-----------------|------------------|
| **Active Memory** | Current state, priorities, hot items | Always | Every session |
| **Seeds** | Compressed summaries of completed/stable items — ~60% smaller, with **every decision, commitment, and outcome preserved** (the full deliberation history moves to Deep). | Always (compact) | When items stabilize |
| **Deep Memory** | Full detail behind seeds. Cold storage. | Never | On retrieval only |

### Self-Correction Layer

- **Tenth Man Rule** — Every session, the AI audits its own context: staleness, contradictions, gaps, changed truths, cascade risks. Based on the Israeli intelligence principle: when everyone agrees, someone must dissent. *(Tier: DP — right-size it: fast triage at session start, full audit weekly.)*
- **Kaizen Engine** — End-of-day continuous improvement. "What should we do differently tomorrow?" Evidence-based, never auto-executes. *(In D/P terms: Kaizen IS the hardening ladder in motion — its log becomes a record of P→DP→D migrations.)*
- **Vault Map** — A purpose-built structural auditor (working tool included in `tools/`): orphans, islands, declared-vs-actual relationship gaps, staleness, heat, hub density — plus an interactive local map. *(Tier: D — the audit never lies.)*

### Operational Index (Level 3)

A routing table: "Given what I'm doing right now, which files should I load?" Prevents loading everything every time. Keeps sessions fast and focused. Its cross-reference matrix doubles as the **declared-relationship source** the Vault Map audits against.

### Document Registry (Level 3)

Intake system for new information. Every document that arrives gets cataloged: what is it, where does it live, what actions are needed, is it the canonical source?

### Action Tracker (Level 3)

A single canonical list of every open action item, surfaced at the start of every session. Before this file exists, actions scatter across priority tables and hide inside session-log prose — and items silently slip. New actions are added the moment they're captured; closed items archive after one session.

### Signal Scan (Level 3)

Most AI context systems are *pull* — you ask, the AI answers. The Signal Scan adds a *push* layer: at session start, the AI proactively reviews your communication channels and surfaces what's relevant to your current priorities, before you have to know to look. **Your SOT priorities ARE the relevance filter** — no separate interest profile to maintain. *(Hybrid by design: collection can be deterministic — see the poller pattern in the guide — while relevance scoring stays probabilistic.)*

### Output Contracts

The steps of your session ritual say *what to gather*; an **output contract** says *what the human actually sees* — a required structure plus an explicit quality bar. Without one, your best-ever session is one lazy session away from regressing into raw tool dumps. Pairs with the **write-verification mandate**: the AI may never claim an external write is "done" until it reads the target back and confirms the change landed. → [`guides/output-contract.md`](guides/output-contract.md)

### Multi-Agent Vault

The vault is also the answer to "Agent A knows something — how does Agent B find out?" ACI v3 separates permissions instead of letting every agent write: **read-only scouts** emit bounded immutable packets; a **local synthesizer** reads routed canon and stages proposals; rare **canonical writers** apply only human-approved diffs within non-overlapping file ownership and verify by read-back. Scheduled agents never write to canon or external systems. Local versioning remains the deterministic recovery layer. → [`guides/multi-agent-vault.md`](guides/multi-agent-vault.md)

### Fork & Onboard (Teams)

A mature vault separates into **architecture** (transferable) and **content** (personal). Forking = copy the structure, zero the content: a new team member starts from a proven skeleton on day one and supplies only what they uniquely know. Includes the hard case — onboarding someone who just absorbed a departed colleague's scope. Share the *how*, not the *what*. → [`guides/fork-and-onboard.md`](guides/fork-and-onboard.md)

---

## Performance Data (Real-World)

| Metric | Level 2 (flat) | Level 3 (relational) | Improvement |
|--------|----------------|---------------------|-------------|
| Lines loaded at session start | ~4,100 | ~1,240 | −70% |
| Time to first useful output | Full parse of everything | Core + route, load on demand | Tracks the −70% lines-loaded figure (~3×) |
| Scaling cost (new entity) | O(n) — grows existing files | O(1) — new file + index entry | Constant |
| Document retrieval | Grep + hope | Registry lookup | Deterministic — *when the intake ritual is followed (itself a DP-tier rule)* |
| Structural integrity | Trust + memory | Vault Map audit | Machine-checked |

*Method: measurements from the production source vault (one practitioner, 40+ sessions). Lines-loaded is counted directly from the session-start read set; "time to first useful output" is reported via its driver — lines parsed — rather than a wall-clock benchmark.*

First run of the Vault Map audit on the mature source vault (28 files, ~200 cross-references): zero orphans and zero islands — the cross-reference discipline held — but **6 declared-vs-actual gaps, 2 of which were real errors** in the index file. The audit pays for itself on day one.

---

## 18 Lessons Learned (40+ Sessions)

1. **Documentation is load-bearing infrastructure** — not optional
2. **If you explained it twice, write it down**
3. **Stale specs are worse than no specs** — update in the same session as changes
4. **One canonical location per fact** — cross-reference everywhere else
5. **Date everything, version everything, flag staleness**
6. **The system must be auditable** — "where does this fact live?" should have exactly one answer
7. **Memory quality > file size** — don't optimize for minimum, optimize for effectiveness
8. **Progressive adoption works** — start Level 1, upgrade when pain appears
9. **Self-correction is non-negotiable** — without Tenth Man, context rots silently
10. **Compression must preserve the whole** — over-fragmenting destroys coherence
11. **A single action tracker beats scattered to-dos.** When open actions live across multiple priority tables and session notes, the *feeling* of "I'm missing something" is usually correct. One canonical, session-surfaced action file fixes it.
12. **Push beats pull for the things you'd otherwise miss.** A pull-only system only surfaces what you think to ask about. A session-start Signal Scan surfaces what you didn't know to look for — which is exactly where things fall through.
13. **Purpose-built beats generic for visualization — because your SOT's semantics ARE the map.** We evaluated pointing Obsidian at the vault and rejected it: a generic graph only knows "files link to files," and demands its own link syntax. Your vault already encodes status heat, freshness, tiers, and *declared* relationships. A ~350-line read-only script renders all of that AND audits declared-vs-actual structure — the drift a generic tool can't even see. Never change your files to please a tool.
14. **Files are the sync layer.** Agent portability and multi-agent memory don't require a service — any agent that reads your vault shares it. Curation (ritual + audit) is what makes shared memory *trustworthy*; accumulation alone just shares the errors around.
15. **Version with git, narrate with footers.** Prose version footers are LLM-maintained and drift; a local git repo (no remote) under the vault gives deterministic diffs and time-travel for free. The hardening ladder applied to versioning itself.
16. **Optimize for correctness, not tokens.** Commercial memory layers minimize token cost because they serve platforms' economics; a personal/team vault's real cost is a wrong fact in production. Spend freely on verification: second passes, read-backs, background audits, defect logging. The most expensive token is the one that was wrong.
17. **Separate observation from authority.** Scouts may collect and summarize, but only a local, human-gated writer may change canon. Permission boundaries are more reliable than asking one powerful agent to remember when not to act.
18. **Unavailable is a first-class result.** A visible `UNAVAILABLE` with a reason protects decisions better than a missing section, guessed value, or stale substitute.

## Who This Is For

- **Managers** with 5+ direct reports and multiple workstreams
- **Consultants** managing multiple client engagements
- **Founders** juggling product, sales, ops, and fundraising
- **Program managers** tracking cross-functional initiatives
- **Anyone** whose AI assistant context has outgrown a single file

---

## Platform Compatibility

The framework is markdown files, so any AI that reads files can participate. But the session ritual has a **write-back half** — the AI updates the vault at session end — and that's where platforms genuinely differ:

| Surface | Reads the vault | Writes it back | Ritual support |
|---------|-----------------|----------------|----------------|
| Local coding or desktop agent with filesystem access | ✅ | ✅ | Full |
| Claude Code / Claude Desktop (filesystem access) | ✅ | ✅ | Full |
| Cursor · Windsurf · AI-enabled editors | ✅ | ✅ | Full |
| Any MCP-compatible agent with filesystem access | ✅ | ✅ | Full |
| claude.ai (Projects / file upload) | ✅ | ❌ — you apply its proposed updates yourself | Read + manual write-back |
| ChatGPT (file upload / memory) | ✅ | ❌ — same | Read + manual write-back |

On chat-only surfaces the system still works: the AI proposes the end-of-session updates and you paste them in. But the compounding benefits arrive fastest where the AI can maintain the files itself. If you live in a chat interface, start at Level 1 and keep the write-back burden small.

**"Why not just use built-in memory?"** claude.ai and ChatGPT both ship native memory now, and it's genuinely useful — zero-effort recall. What it can't give you is a memory you can **read, diff, version, audit, and carry between vendors**. Built-in memory is per-app and opaque; a vault is portable, inspectable, git-versioned, shareable across every agent you use, and curated under an explicit discipline. The two compose fine: let built-in memory handle casual recall while the vault remains canon.

---

## Quick Start

1. Copy `templates/level-1-single-file.md` to your working directory
2. Fill in the sections with your current context
3. At the start of every AI session, tell your assistant to read the file
4. At the end of every session, ask your assistant to update it *(on chat-only platforms, apply its proposed updates yourself)*
5. When it gets unwieldy (~500+ lines), upgrade to Level 2
6. As rules accumulate, tag each one **D / DP / P** — and let your weekly review ask which DP rules are ready to harden down the ladder
7. Optional: when manual preparation is stable, use the disabled-by-default [`control-panel-config.yaml`](templates/control-panel-config.yaml) and follow the [Control Panel checklist](guides/control-panel-checklist.md) through shadow and canary stages

---

## Philosophy

> **"89.6% of AI tokens are wasted re-reading context that could be managed."**

That figure is **our own measurement, not a borrowed stat**: in a controlled 50-conversation study across 5 work domains, managed context matched frontier-model output quality at ~89% lower token cost (n=50, p<0.001). The average AI conversation spends most of its capacity re-establishing context that was already known. This framework eliminates that waste by giving the AI a persistent, structured, self-maintaining memory system.

And as the system matures, the philosophy sharpens: **probabilistic AI interprets and judges; deterministic infrastructure executes and verifies.** The AI becomes a true partner — not a stranger you brief from scratch every time, and not a black box you have to blindly trust either.

# Level 2 Setup: Multi-File SOT Architecture

> **When to read this:** Your single-file SOT has grown unwieldy (500+ lines) or you're managing multiple domains.  
> **Time required:** 45–60 minutes to migrate  
> **Outcome:** 4–5 specialized files that are faster to read, easier to update, and less likely to rot.

---

## Signals It's Time to Upgrade

You need Level 2 when you notice any of these:

- **File > 500 lines** — Your AI is spending context window on irrelevant sections
- **Scrolling to find things** — You can't quickly locate what you need
- **AI missing context** — Important details buried in a wall of text
- **Multiple domains** — Work, side projects, personal goals all in one file
- **Update anxiety** — You hesitate to add things because the file is already too long

If you're experiencing 2+ of these, it's time.

---

## The Level 2 Architecture

Split your single file into 4–5 specialized documents:

```
~/my-brain/
├── source-of-truth.md        # Current state, priorities, session log
├── people-reference.md        # All people, relationships, org context
├── projects-reference.md      # Active projects, milestones, decisions
├── recipes-playbook.md        # Procedures, data sources, how-to's
└── quality-contract.md        # (Optional) Standards, thresholds, rules
```

Each file has a single responsibility. No file should need to duplicate content from another.

---

## What Goes Where (Decision Tree)

When you're not sure where something belongs, use this:

```
Is it about a PERSON or RELATIONSHIP?
  → people-reference.md

Is it a PROCEDURE or RECIPE (how to do something)?
  → recipes-playbook.md

Is it a PROJECT with milestones, decisions, or deliverables?
  → projects-reference.md

Is it about CURRENT STATE, PRIORITIES, or SESSION HISTORY?
  → source-of-truth.md

Is it a RULE, THRESHOLD, or QUALITY STANDARD?
  → quality-contract.md
```

**When in doubt:** Put it in source-of-truth.md and move it later. Better to capture than to lose.

---

## Migration Steps

### Step 1: Create the new files (10 min)

Create empty files with headers for each section. Use the Level 2 templates if available, or create your own structure:

```markdown
# People Reference
Last updated: 2024-06-01

## Core Team
## Stakeholders  
## External Contacts
## Org Context & Transitions
```

### Step 2: Move content from your single file (20 min)

Go through your existing SOT section by section:
- **Cut** content from the single file
- **Paste** into the appropriate specialized file
- **Add context** if needed (a sentence that made sense in the original might need a header in the new location)

### Step 3: Add cross-references (5 min)

Where content in one file relates to another, add a pointer:

```markdown
## Platform Migration
Status: 60% complete, deadline Sept 15
Tech lead: Priya Patel (see people-reference.md)
Runbook: see recipes-playbook.md § Migration Procedures
```

### Step 4: Update your session instructions (5 min)

Change your AI's startup instruction to read ALL files:

```
At the start of every session:
1. Read all files in ~/my-brain/
2. Briefly acknowledge current state
3. Surface upcoming deadlines or open items
```

### Step 5: Validate (10 min)

Start a new session. Does your AI have full context? Can it answer:
- "What am I working on?" (source-of-truth.md)
- "Who is Marcus?" (people-reference.md)
- "What's the migration status?" (projects-reference.md)
- "How do I run the deploy?" (recipes-playbook.md)

If anything is missing, it fell through a crack during migration.

---

## Cross-Referencing Rules

The most important rule in a multi-file system:

> **Every fact lives in ONE canonical location. Everywhere else gets a pointer.**

### Why This Matters

If "Priya is the migration tech lead" appears in both `people-reference.md` and `projects-reference.md`, they will eventually contradict each other. One will get updated, the other won't.

### How to Do It

**Canonical location** — where the full detail lives:
```markdown
# people-reference.md
## Priya Patel
- Role: Senior Engineer, Tech Lead on Platform Migration
- Reports to: Marcus Webb
- Working style: Deep focus, prefers Slack over meetings
- Note: Overloaded in Q3 — shield from non-essential meetings
```

**Pointer** — in other files that reference this person:
```markdown
# projects-reference.md
## Platform Migration
- Tech Lead: Priya Patel (→ people-reference.md)
```

### Decision: Where Is Canonical?

| Information Type | Canonical Location |
|-----------------|-------------------|
| Person's role, style, relationships | people-reference.md |
| Project status, milestones, decisions | projects-reference.md |
| How to do something | recipes-playbook.md |
| Current priorities, state | source-of-truth.md |
| Rules, thresholds | quality-contract.md |

---

## Session Ritual Changes

Your session ritual evolves at Level 2:

### Session Start
1. AI reads **all** SOT files (not just one)
2. AI acknowledges current state and surfaces relevant items
3. AI notes any staleness or contradictions across files

### Session End
1. AI updates **only the affected files** (not all of them)
2. Session log entry goes in source-of-truth.md
3. AI checks: did new info get added to the right canonical location?
4. Timestamps updated on changed files

### Example End-of-Session Update

> "Today we discussed the migration timeline change. I've updated:
> - `projects-reference.md` — new deadline (Sept 22), added risk note
> - `source-of-truth.md` — session log entry, updated priority #1
> - `people-reference.md` — no changes needed"

---

## Tips for Level 2

1. **Don't over-split.** 4–5 files is the sweet spot. More than 7 and you'll lose coherence.

2. **Keep source-of-truth.md as the "home base."** It should always answer: "What's happening right now?"

3. **Version your files.** Add `Last updated: YYYY-MM-DD` at the top of each file. Stale dates are a smell.

4. **Review monthly.** Once a month, read all files front-to-back. Archive completed projects. Remove departed people.

5. **Trust the system.** It feels weird at first to split things up. After 2 weeks, you won't go back.

---

## When to Upgrade to Level 3

You're ready for Level 3 when:
- Individual files exceed ~1000 lines
- Loading everything at session start is slow or wasteful
- Entities (projects, people, vendors) need their own dedicated files
- New information arrives faster than you can organize it
- You need memory tiers (active vs. archived)

**Next:** Read `level-3-migration.md` for the advanced architecture.

---

*Level 2 is where most people should stay. It handles complex professional lives with multiple projects and dozens of stakeholders. Only upgrade to Level 3 if you're hitting real limits.*

# Guide: The Action Tracker

> One canonical list of open actions, surfaced every session start.

## The Problem

In a Level 3 system, your open action items naturally end up scattered:

- Some in your **source-of-truth priority tables** (P0, This Week, Watchlist...)
- Some buried inside **session-log prose** ("...send the deck by Friday")
- Some only in **a meeting's notes**
- Some only in **your head**

Each location is individually reasonable. Collectively, they guarantee one thing: you
will *feel* like you're forgetting something — and you'll be right. There is no single
surface that answers "what do I actually owe right now?"

## The Fix

A dedicated **Action Tracker** core file (`action-tracker.md`) that is:

1. **Canonical** — the one place open actions live.
2. **An extract, not a replacement** — full context stays in your SOT priority tiers;
   this is the scannable "to-do" layer pulled from them.
3. **Surfaced every session start** — the AI reads it and leads the session brief with
   your open 🔴 / 🟠 items.
4. **Continuously maintained** — the moment an action is captured anywhere in a session,
   the AI also writes it here. Closed items are marked done and archived next session.

## Why It Works

- **Single source of scan.** You look in one place, every day. No reconciliation across
  five tables.
- **The AI owns upkeep.** You don't maintain a separate to-do app that drifts out of
  sync. The tracker is updated as a side effect of normal session work.
- **Status at a glance.** The 🔴/🟠/🟡/🟢/⏸️ taxonomy means you instantly see what's on
  fire vs. parked vs. waiting on someone.
- **Deferred ≠ dropped.** The ⏸️ status captures "I can't act until X" so blocked items
  stay visible instead of silently vanishing.

## Setup

1. Copy `templates/level-3-action-tracker.md` into your system as `action-tracker.md`.
2. **Seed it once:** ask your AI to sweep your existing SOT priority tables AND your
   recent session logs and compile every open action you own into the tracker. (This
   first compile is usually eye-opening — expect more items than you thought.)
3. **Wire it into your session ritual / router** so it's read at the start of every
   session and surfaced as an "Open Actions" block.
4. **Add a maintenance rule to your quality file:** "Any newly-captured action item is
   written to the Action Tracker in the same session. Closed items are marked done and
   archived at the next session."

## Status Taxonomy

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| 🔴 | Overdue or urgent — blocking someone, or past due |
| 🟠 | Active this week — you intend to move it now |
| 🟡 | Open, no deadline — real but not time-boxed |
| 🟢 | Done — keep one session for visibility, then archive |
| ⏸️ | Deferred — waiting on a person, event, or upstream decision |

## What NOT to Put Here

- **Fully delegated items.** If someone else owns it end-to-end, it lives in their entity
  file. Only put it here if *you* have an action on it.
- **Full context.** Keep rows terse. The "why" lives in your SOT; link to it via the
  cross-reference column.
- **Reference material.** This is actions, not notes.

## The Payoff

The first time you run a clean session start and your AI opens with *"Here are your 3 red
and 7 amber open actions"* — pulled automatically, every day — the scattered-to-do
anxiety disappears. You stop wondering what you forgot, because there's one place that
always knows.

# Multi-Agent Vault — One Canon, Different Permissions

The vault can coordinate multiple agents without becoming a shared free-for-all.
ACI v3.0 makes the central distinction explicit:

- a **read-only scout** observes one allowlisted source slice and emits an
  immutable packet; and
- a **canonical writer** applies a human-approved local diff to designated vault
  files and verifies the result.

Most agents should be scouts or local read-only synthesizers. Canonical writers
are exceptional, local, narrow, and human-gated. No scheduled agent writes to
the vault or an external system.

```text
scheduled trigger → orchestrator → read-only scout → immutable packet
                                                    ↓
local vault (read only) → local synthesizer → sealed brief + proposed diff
                                                    ↓
                                         human approval gate
                                                    ↓
                                      local canonical writer
                                                    ↓
                                         read-back verification
```

This separation keeps collection portable while preserving one trusted local
canon. Different models and runtimes can participate because the contract lives
in files and packets, not in one vendor's memory service.

## Agent roles

| Role | Reads | Writes | Typical lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read-only scout | One allowlisted source through one narrow skill | One immutable packet to the packet sink | Scheduled or on demand |
| Packet validator | Incoming packet, schema, and allowlist policy | Acceptance or quarantine metadata | Event-driven |
| Local synthesizer | Accepted packets and routed vault files | Sealed brief and proposed diff in staging | Scheduled or on demand |
| Canonical writer | Human-approved diff and owned vault files | Approved local vault files | On demand only |
| Live-delta reader | Small allowlisted source window | Labeled delta view | Human-initiated and bounded |
| External actor | Approved instruction and one target | One external change, followed by read-back | Human-initiated only; outside scheduled collection |

An agent may hold only one of these capability profiles during a run. In
particular, do not combine scout and canonical-writer credentials.

## Read-only scouts

A scout does not read the full vault. It receives only:

- a purpose-built job instruction;
- source and field aliases from a deny-by-default allowlist;
- a bounded time window and result limit;
- a short-lived read credential; and
- the packet contract for its one output type.

It cannot call arbitrary source APIs, broaden a query, write back to the source,
or update local canon. Its output excludes raw transcripts, complete messages,
attachment bytes, credentials, private links, provider record identifiers,
prompt traces, and vault content.

A cloud scout is acceptable only when its task needs no vault context and its
minimal packet is approved for remote processing. Never upload the entire vault
to make a cloud scout convenient.

## Local synthesizers

A synthesizer is read-only with respect to canon. The operational index routes it
to only the vault files needed for the brief. It combines those files with
accepted, schema-validated packets and produces:

1. an immutable sealed brief with packet references and status; and
2. if canon may need an update, an exact proposed diff in a staging directory.

The synthesizer does not apply its own proposal. Separating proposal from
execution makes review meaningful and preserves the deterministic write gate.

## Canonical writers

A canonical writer is a local capability, not a general agent personality. It
receives one approved diff, an explicit file scope, and no source credentials.
It must:

1. confirm the approval refers to the exact diff and current file versions;
2. reject files outside its ownership partition;
3. apply the change locally;
4. read the changed files back;
5. verify required new content is present and replaced content is gone;
6. report `READY`, `DEGRADED`, or `BLOCKED` for the write result; and
7. leave external publication to a separate explicit action.

If read-back cannot run, the result is not `READY`. The writer reports the
change as unverified and the workflow is `DEGRADED` or `BLOCKED` according to
whether the unverified write can be safely ignored or must be reversed.

## Coordination rules

### Rule 1 — Default every agent to read-only

Start with no write capability. Add a canonical writer only when a demonstrated
workflow requires it, and keep human approval between synthesis and execution.
An agent that cannot reliably follow the quality contract remains read-only.

### Rule 2 — Partition canonical write ownership by file

Two canonical writers must never own the same file. Partition ownership by file
or directory and record it in the operational index. Reads are routed by need;
writes are restricted by ownership.

### Rule 3 — One canonical owner for the master action list

Actions are a high-collision surface. Designate exactly one canonical writer for
the action tracker. Scouts and specialist agents surface candidate actions in
packets or proposed diffs; they never write the tracker directly.

### Rule 4 — Scope specialists narrowly

A specialist gets its routed project files or source skill, not the whole vault.
A narrow context protects unrelated canon and preserves attention for the task.

### Rule 5 — Use one contract for all proposals and writes

Every proposed change names the target files, exact diff, basis packets, as-of
time, and expected verification. Every canonical write follows the same
approval and read-back rules, regardless of model or runtime.

### Rule 6 — Keep external writes out of the scheduled path

A scheduled trigger may lead to a packet and sealed brief, never to a sent
message, changed source record, published document, or canonical vault update.
An external action needs its own human approval, least-privilege tool, and
read-back verification.

## Collision and stale-base handling

A proposal records the digest or version of every target file it read. If a
target changed before approval, the writer rejects the stale proposal. The
synthesizer must rebuild it against current canon; the writer never attempts an
LLM-generated merge while holding write permission.

Use atomic local writes where possible: write a temporary file, validate it,
then replace the target. A partial multi-file write is `BLOCKED`; roll back to
the pre-approved versions and report which files were verified.

## Handoffs

A safe handoff contains curated state, not session history:

- purpose and bounded scope;
- packet or sealed-brief references;
- explicit assumptions and unavailable inputs;
- candidate actions or proposed diff;
- required human decision; and
- expiry or freshness time.

Do not hand off raw transcripts. The receiving agent reads current canon and the
bounded handoff rather than inheriting another agent's full context window.

## Local versioning

Use local version control or another local snapshot mechanism beneath prose
version notes. Do not configure a remote for a vault containing sensitive
context. Before a canonical write, capture the current local version; after the
write, record the verified diff. This supplies deterministic recovery without
turning a cloud repository into a context store.

## Minimum safe adoption

1. Inventory agents and classify each one by the role table above.
2. Remove write scopes from all scheduled and source-reading agents.
3. Create source allowlists and narrow skills for scouts.
4. Route accepted packets to a local read-only synthesizer.
5. Put proposed changes in staging, never in the canonical vault.
6. Assign non-overlapping files to the few canonical writers that remain.
7. Require exact-diff approval and read-back verification.
8. Test stale-base rejection, partial-write rollback, and the schedule kill
   switch before enabling automation.

For packet details, see [Packet Contract](packet-contract.md). For scheduling and
retries, see [Scheduled Agents](scheduled-agents.md). For status rendering, see
[The Output Contract](output-contract.md).

# Scheduled Agents — Safe Collection Without Autonomous Action

Scheduled agents make ACI proactive, but they also introduce a new trust
boundary. In v3.0, every scheduled agent is a **read-only scout**: it collects a
small allowlisted slice, emits an immutable packet, and stops. It cannot write to
the canonical vault or any external source.

Use this guide with [ACI Control Panel](control-panel.md) and the
[`control-panel-config.yaml`](../templates/control-panel-config.yaml) template.

## Role boundaries

| Role | Location | Capability |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | Scheduler | Emits time and schedule metadata only |
| Orchestrator | Control plane | Authorizes, deduplicates, dispatches, retries, and records state |
| Scout | Cloud or local runtime | Reads one allowlisted source through one narrow skill; emits one packet |
| Validator | Packet boundary | Validates, hashes, accepts, or quarantines |
| Synthesizer | Local runtime | Reads accepted packets and routed vault files; creates a sealed brief and optional proposed patch |
| Canonical writer | Local, human-gated | Applies an approved diff to designated vault files and reads it back |

Do not combine scout and canonical-writer credentials. A process that can both
read a broad source and write canon defeats the safety model.

## Designing a schedule

Every schedule declares:

- a stable schedule name;
- a timezone and daylight-saving policy;
- the intended trigger expression;
- one packet type;
- one scout job and runtime class;
- required source skills;
- maximum execution time;
- freshness deadline;
- retry policy;
- packet size and record-count limits; and
- whether the schedule is disabled, shadow, canary, or active.

A schedule is not permission. The job still needs a source allowlist and a
read-only credential.

### Choose cloud or local deliberately

Use a cloud runtime when the approved source is already remote, the packet can be
minimal, and no vault context is required. Use a local runtime when collection
needs local-only material or policy prohibits remote processing. In both cases,
the scout remains narrow and read-only. The canonical vault is never uploaded to
make a cloud job easier.

## Narrow source skills

A source skill is safer than a general-purpose connector because its interface
expresses the job's maximum scope. A good skill accepts only bounded parameters,
for example:

```text
read_summary(source_alias, window_start, window_end, fields)
```

The implementation checks all four parameters against configuration. It should
not expose arbitrary query text, arbitrary URLs, “read all,” or write methods.
Prefer aggregate or summary endpoints. Apply field filtering at the source and a
second redaction pass before packet creation.

Each skill has a deny-by-default allowlist:

- approved source aliases;
- approved resource aliases within each source;
- approved fields;
- maximum lookback and lookahead;
- maximum records and bytes; and
- allowed packet types.

## Orchestration and idempotency

Compute an idempotency key from stable control-plane facts:

```text
schedule name + intended run time + packet type + config version
```

Store one terminal result per key. The intended run time does not change during
a retry or manual replay. Required behavior:

| Situation | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Same key, same request, run active | Return current run state; do not dispatch again |
| Same key, same request, run complete | Return existing result and packet reference |
| Same key, different request | Reject as a conflict and alert |
| New key | Create one run and dispatch once |

Packet acceptance and sealed-brief creation use the same principle. Idempotency
must cover the whole route, not only job dispatch.

## Retries and failure classes

Use exponential backoff with jitter and a low attempt cap. Retry only transient
errors:

| Category | Retry? | Result after final attempt |
|---|---|---|
| Temporary network failure | Yes | Explicit `SOURCE_UNREACHABLE` |
| Rate limit with safe retry time | Yes | Explicit `SOURCE_UNREACHABLE` |
| Runtime interruption before packet acceptance | Yes, same key | Resume or return existing result |
| Permission denied | No | `PERMISSION_DENIED`; alert operator |
| Source outside allowlist | No | Policy rejection; `BLOCKED` |
| Schema or semantic validation failure | No | Quarantine; `VALIDATION_FAILED` |
| Reporting period not closed | No | `NOT_CLOSED`; follow period policy |
| Attempted write or permission expansion | No | Stop, revoke, and investigate |

Do not let retries broaden a query, increase the time window, switch sources, or
drop validation requirements.

## Observability without surveillance

Record enough metadata to operate the system, not enough content to recreate the
source. A run log may contain:

- schedule, job, skill, source alias, and config version;
- intended, start, and finish timestamps;
- attempt number, duration, and state transition;
- aggregate records observed and packet bytes;
- packet digest and validation reason codes; and
- freshness age and seal result.

It must not contain raw messages, full source responses, vault excerpts,
credentials, private resource links, provider record identifiers, prompts that
embed canonical content, or packet payload copies.

Useful service indicators include schedule success rate, duplicate suppression,
retry rate, packet quarantine rate, freshness lag, synthesis latency, and count
of briefs by `READY` / `DEGRADED` / `BLOCKED`.

## Human approval and external effects

A scheduled path ends at a packet or sealed brief. It never:

- sends or edits a message;
- updates a ticket, calendar item, financial system, or document;
- approves a transaction;
- changes access controls;
- writes directly to canonical vault files; or
- publishes a brief.

The local synthesizer may create a proposed patch in staging. A human reviews
the exact diff, approves its file scope, and invokes the canonical writer. The
writer reads the target back before reporting success. External writes require a
separate, explicit human action and are outside the scheduled collection path.

## Missed and late schedules

A late job keeps its original `scheduled_for` timestamp and declares its actual
`produced_at`. The brief evaluates freshness from both. Do not relabel a late
packet as current.

If a schedule is missed:

1. mark the expected packet unavailable;
2. derive `DEGRADED` or `BLOCKED` from the output contract;
3. alert with content-free metadata;
4. allow a manual replay with the original intended time; and
5. do not silently substitute a packet from another period.

## Bounded live delta

A live delta is a separate, on-demand read after a brief is sealed. Configure all
bounds in advance:

- disabled by default;
- human-initiated only;
- allowlisted skills only;
- lookback beginning no earlier than the seal time, subject to a small maximum;
- maximum calls and records;
- short wall-clock timeout; and
- no writes or vault mutation.

Render the delta under its own heading with query time, source aliases, and
status. “No change observed” is valid only when every required delta source was
reachable; otherwise list unavailable sources.

## Safe rollout

1. Validate configuration and packet fixtures locally.
2. Run the job manually with synthetic or non-sensitive test data.
3. Enable **shadow** mode: collect and validate, but do not synthesize.
4. Compare packet summaries with the approved manual source.
5. Enable one **canary** schedule with operator review.
6. Measure freshness, duplicate suppression, retries, and quarantines.
7. Expand one source and one schedule at a time.

## Rollback checklist

- [ ] Disable the affected schedule.
- [ ] Revoke or suspend its credential if policy may have been breached.
- [ ] Stop promotion from incoming to accepted packets.
- [ ] Preserve accepted packets and sealed briefs as immutable evidence.
- [ ] Restore the previous versioned config, schema, and skill package.
- [ ] Re-run validation before re-enabling shadow mode.
- [ ] Confirm no canonical vault or external write occurred autonomously.

# Financial Health — Closed Baselines and Honest Freshness

The financial-health packet and brief are designed to answer three different
questions without blending them:

1. **YTD through the prior closed month:** What is the cumulative closed-year
   position?
2. **Prior-month close:** What did the most recently closed month contribute?
3. **Month to date (MTD):** What preliminary movement is visible now?

Every financial-health output must render all three sections in that order. A
section without a usable value is still rendered with `UNAVAILABLE`, an explicit
reason, and its intended reporting window. Never omit it, replace it with zero,
or silently substitute an older period.

See the generic packet fixture in
[`templates/financial-health-packet.json`](../templates/financial-health-packet.json).

## Define the close calendar first

“Prior month” means the most recent month marked closed by the approved close
calendar—not simply the calendar month before today. Configuration must declare:

- reporting timezone;
- fiscal-year start;
- currency and unit;
- accounting basis used by the approved summary;
- close-calendar source alias;
- freshness threshold for closed and preliminary data; and
- treatment of post-close adjustments.

If the calendar says the expected month is not closed, use `NOT_CLOSED`. Do not
promote preliminary values into a closed baseline.

## Required period objects

### YTD through prior closed month

Required fields:

- label: `YTD through prior closed month`;
- fiscal-year start date;
- end date equal to the prior closed month's end date;
- availability and optional unavailable reason;
- approved metric set with unit and value when available; and
- close-calendar confirmation.

### Prior-month close

Required fields:

- label: `Prior-month close`;
- start and end dates of the same prior closed month used by YTD;
- availability and optional unavailable reason;
- the same core metric keys and units used in YTD; and
- closed status.

### Month to date

Required fields:

- label: `Month to date`;
- start of the current reporting month;
- as-of date and timestamp;
- availability and optional unavailable reason;
- preliminary status; and
- the same core metric keys and units when the source provides them.

If the approved source does not provide MTD, render for example:

```json
{
  "label": "Month to date",
  "start_date": "2030-05-01",
  "end_date": "2030-05-15",
  "availability": "UNAVAILABLE",
  "unavailable_reason": "NOT_PROVIDED",
  "note": "The approved source does not provide MTD values."
}
```

This is a valid explicit limitation, not a missing field.

## Status rules

Financial-health status is deliberately conservative:

| Condition | Brief state |
|---|---|
| All three sections available, fresh, validated, and comparable | `READY` |
| Closed YTD and prior-month close are valid; MTD is explicitly unavailable with a reason | `READY` — limitation remains visible |
| MTD is present but stale, partial, or otherwise limited | `DEGRADED` |
| YTD through prior closed month is unavailable or invalid | `BLOCKED` |
| Prior-month close is unavailable, not closed, or uses a mismatched basis | `BLOCKED` |
| Period dates disagree, arithmetic fails, currency/unit is ambiguous, or source is outside allowlist | `BLOCKED` |

A `DEGRADED` financial brief must put the limitation above the first number. A
`BLOCKED` brief still shows the three headings and reasons, but must not present a
headline decision metric as trustworthy.

## Metric shape

Each available metric should carry:

```json
{
  "value": 100000,
  "unit": "USD",
  "availability": "AVAILABLE"
}
```

Use one stable metric dictionary across periods. Generic deployments commonly
include inflow, outflow, and net, but the operator must define the approved
terms. Do not infer accounting meanings from labels alone.

Preserve numeric values as numbers, not formatted strings. Formatting belongs in
the sealed brief. If rounding is applied, declare the scale and rounding rule.

## Deterministic validation

Before acceptance, verify:

1. The prior-month close is marked closed by the approved calendar.
2. YTD ends on the exact same date as the prior-month close.
3. Prior-month dates form one complete reporting month.
4. MTD starts on the current reporting month's first date and ends on the packet
   as-of date.
5. Periods use the same currency, unit scale, and accounting basis.
6. Required metric keys exist when a section is `AVAILABLE`.
7. Net arithmetic follows the deployment's declared formula.
8. Aggregated YTD and month values pass approved reconciliation tolerances.
9. The source alias is allowlisted and data is within freshness thresholds.
10. Every unavailable section has an allowed reason and no fake substitute value.

A schema pass is not enough; these are semantic checks.

## Source minimization

The financial scout reads an approved aggregate summary, not transaction-level
records. Its credential is read-only and limited to the configured reporting
period and fields. Packets must not include account numbers, transaction IDs,
customer data, credentials, internal resource links, or raw ledger exports.

When aggregation is unavailable at the source, calculate locally or add an
approved summary view. Do not send the local vault or a detailed ledger to a
cloud scout.

## Sealed-brief presentation

A financial-health section in a sealed brief should contain:

1. status and as-of line;
2. limitations, if any;
3. YTD through prior closed month;
4. prior-month close;
5. MTD or explicit unavailable state;
6. material changes using a declared comparison basis;
7. validation notes; and
8. packet references and seal time.

Label MTD as preliminary. Never compare preliminary MTD directly with a full
closed month without a clearly named normalization method. Avoid unsupported
forecasting; a trend observation is not a forecast.

## Corrections and late close

A post-close adjustment creates a new financial packet with a new digest and a
`supersedes_packet_id`. It does not edit the prior packet or sealed brief. The
next sealed brief states that a newer close packet superseded the earlier one.

If close occurs late, the output remains `BLOCKED` with `NOT_CLOSED` for the
closed sections until an accepted packet confirms closure. Do not advance the
YTD endpoint based on the date alone.

## Review checklist

- [ ] All three period headings are present.
- [ ] YTD and prior-month close share the same closed endpoint.
- [ ] MTD is present or explicitly `UNAVAILABLE`.
- [ ] Currency, unit, basis, and date windows are visible.
- [ ] Preliminary and closed values are clearly distinguished.
- [ ] Status follows the conservative rules above.
- [ ] No transaction-level or identifying data entered the packet.
- [ ] Packet digest and immutable history are intact.

### Start of Session
1. Read all Level 2 documents (source-of-truth, people, projects, recipes, quality)
2. Acknowledge review: "I've reviewed your SOT — here's where we left off..."
3. Surface relevant context: upcoming deadlines, open items, priority shifts
4. Run Tenth Man audit (see `level-2-quality.md#tenth-man-rule`)
5. Ask: "What are we working on today?" (unless task is already clear)

### End of Session
1. Update affected SOT documents with any new information
2. Add session log entry to `level-2-source-of-truth.md#session-log`
3. Update "Last updated" timestamps on changed documents
4. Check cross-references — new info lives in ONE canonical place with refs elsewhere
5. Run Tenth Man audit (end-of-session pass)
6. If last session of the business day → run Kaizen review (see `level-2-quality.md#kaizen`)
7. Confirm SOT updates with user

## Hard Rules

<!-- 
  Non-negotiable operational rules. These override everything else.
  Keep this list short and absolute.
-->

- **ALWAYS** read SOT documents at session start — no exceptions
- **ALWAYS** update session log before ending a session
- **NEVER** make up information — say "I don't know" or "let me check"
- **NEVER** delete SOT content without explicit permission
- **ALWAYS** flag when information might be stale (>2 weeks without update)
- **ALWAYS** ask before taking irreversible actions (sending messages, deleting files)
- **NEVER** store sensitive credentials in SOT files

## Meeting Prep Recipe

<!-- 
  Standard procedure for preparing for any meeting. AI should offer to run this
  when a meeting is mentioned or approaching.
-->

### Inputs Needed
- Meeting name/type
- Attendees
- Agenda (if available)
- Your goal for the meeting

### Procedure
1. **Pull people context** — Look up all attendees in `level-2-people.md`
2. **Pull project context** — Check `level-2-projects.md` for relevant initiatives
3. **Review last interaction** — Check session log for recent mentions of attendees/topics
4. **Draft prep brief:**
   - Attendee context & communication preferences
   - Relevant project status updates
   - Your talking points aligned to your goal
   - Questions to ask
   - Decisions needed
5. **Post-meeting:** Capture action items, update relevant SOT docs

# ACI Control Panel v3.0 — generic starter configuration
# Copy this file outside the repository and customize aliases and local paths.
# Never place credentials, private links, provider resource IDs, raw content, or
# canonical vault content in this file.

version: "3.0"
display_name: "ACI Control Panel"
environment: "local"
reporting_timezone: "Etc/UTC"
config_revision: "starter-1"

control_plane:
  default_deny: true
  content_free_logs: true
  secrets_from_environment_only: true
  schedules_kill_switch: true
  store_source_payloads: false

storage:
  # All paths are local and must resolve inside the operator's approved workspace.
  packet_root: "./runtime/control-panel/packets"
  incoming: "./runtime/control-panel/packets/incoming"
  accepted_append_only: "./runtime/control-panel/packets/accepted"
  quarantine: "./runtime/control-panel/packets/quarantine"
  sealed_briefs: "./runtime/control-panel/sealed-briefs"
  proposed_changes: "./runtime/control-panel/proposed-changes"
  cloud_vault_storage_allowed: false
  packet_retention_days: 30
  sealed_brief_retention_days: 90

authentication:
  credential_mode: "short_lived"
  separate_identity_per_skill: true
  scout_write_scopes_allowed: false
  credentials_in_config_allowed: false

source_allowlist:
  - alias: "approved_schedule_summary"
    enabled: false
    access: "read_only"
    runtime: "cloud_or_local"
    allowed_skills:
      - "schedule_summary_reader"
    allowed_fields:
      - "time_window"
      - "event_category"
      - "preparation_required"
    maximum_lookback_hours: 24
    maximum_lookahead_hours: 24
    maximum_records: 50
    maximum_response_bytes: 65536
    raw_content_allowed: false
    attachments_allowed: false
    source_record_identifiers_allowed: false

  - alias: "approved_financial_summary"
    enabled: false
    access: "read_only"
    runtime: "cloud_or_local"
    allowed_skills:
      - "financial_summary_reader"
      - "close_calendar_reader"
    allowed_fields:
      - "reporting_period"
      - "close_status"
      - "inflow"
      - "outflow"
      - "net"
      - "currency"
      - "unit_scale"
    maximum_lookback_hours: 9600
    maximum_lookahead_hours: 0
    maximum_records: 100
    maximum_response_bytes: 65536
    raw_content_allowed: false
    transaction_records_allowed: false
    source_record_identifiers_allowed: false

skills:
  schedule_summary_reader:
    enabled: false
    role: "read_only_scout"
    packet_types:
      - "schedule_summary"
    arbitrary_queries_allowed: false
    writes_allowed: false

  financial_summary_reader:
    enabled: false
    role: "read_only_scout"
    packet_types:
      - "financial_health"
    aggregate_only: true
    arbitrary_queries_allowed: false
    writes_allowed: false

  close_calendar_reader:
    enabled: false
    role: "read_only_scout"
    packet_types:
      - "financial_health"
    aggregate_only: true
    arbitrary_queries_allowed: false
    writes_allowed: false

jobs:
  daily_schedule_packet:
    enabled: false
    mode: "shadow"
    runtime: "cloud_or_local"
    source_aliases:
      - "approved_schedule_summary"
    skills:
      - "schedule_summary_reader"
    packet_type: "schedule_summary"
    timeout_seconds: 60
    maximum_packet_bytes: 65536
    maximum_packet_records: 50

  financial_health_packet:
    enabled: false
    mode: "shadow"
    runtime: "cloud_or_local"
    source_aliases:
      - "approved_financial_summary"
    skills:
      - "financial_summary_reader"
      - "close_calendar_reader"
    packet_type: "financial_health"
    timeout_seconds: 90
    maximum_packet_bytes: 65536
    maximum_packet_records: 100
    financial_periods_required:
      - "ytd_through_prior_closed_month"
      - "prior_month_close"
      - "month_to_date_or_explicit_unavailable"

schedules:
  daily_schedule_summary:
    enabled: false
    mode: "shadow"
    job: "daily_schedule_packet"
    cron: "0 6 * * *"
    timezone: "Etc/UTC"
    freshness_deadline_minutes: 120

  monthly_financial_health:
    enabled: false
    mode: "shadow"
    job: "financial_health_packet"
    cron: "0 7 * * *"
    timezone: "Etc/UTC"
    freshness_deadline_minutes: 180

orchestrator:
  idempotency:
    enabled: true
    key_fields:
      - "schedule_name"
      - "scheduled_for"
      - "packet_type"
      - "config_revision"
    conflict_policy: "reject_and_alert"
  retries:
    maximum_attempts: 3
    strategy: "exponential_backoff_with_jitter"
    initial_delay_seconds: 5
    maximum_delay_seconds: 60
    transient_categories:
      - "temporary_network_failure"
      - "rate_limited"
      - "runtime_interrupted_before_acceptance"
    never_retry_categories:
      - "permission_denied"
      - "allowlist_rejection"
      - "schema_validation_failed"
      - "semantic_validation_failed"
      - "attempted_write"

packet_contract:
  schema_path: "./templates/packet.schema.json"
  schema_version: "3.0"
  reject_unknown_top_level_fields: true
  reject_duplicate_json_keys: true
  immutable_after_acceptance: true
  correction_mode: "new_packet_with_supersedes_reference"
  digest:
    algorithm: "SHA-256"
    canonicalization: "sorted-keys-compact-json-without-integrity"
  forbidden_content:
    - "raw_transcripts"
    - "full_message_bodies"
    - "attachment_bytes"
    - "credentials"
    - "private_resource_links"
    - "provider_source_identifiers"
    - "prompt_traces"
    - "canonical_vault_content"

synthesis:
  runtime: "local_only"
  canonical_vault_access: "read_only"
  packet_input: "accepted_only"
  output: "sealed_brief"
  status_values:
    - "READY"
    - "DEGRADED"
    - "BLOCKED"
  unavailable_values_must_be_explicit: true
  proposed_changes_directory: "./runtime/control-panel/proposed-changes"
  autonomous_vault_writes_allowed: false
  autonomous_external_writes_allowed: false

canonical_writer:
  runtime: "local_only"
  enabled: false
  human_approval_required: true
  exact_diff_required: true
  file_scope_required: true
  external_writes_allowed: false
  read_back_verification_required: true

live_delta:
  enabled_by_default: false
  human_initiated_only: true
  source_allowlist_required: true
  maximum_lookback_minutes: 120
  maximum_calls: 3
  maximum_records: 25
  timeout_seconds: 30
  writes_allowed: false
  may_modify_sealed_brief: false
  may_modify_canonical_vault: false

observability:
  metadata_only: true
  record:
    - "scheduled_for"
    - "started_at"
    - "finished_at"
    - "config_revision"
    - "schema_version"
    - "source_alias"
    - "skill_name"
    - "attempt_count"
    - "terminal_state"
    - "records_observed"
    - "fields_emitted"
    - "packet_bytes"
    - "validation_reason_codes"
    - "packet_digest"
    - "sealed_brief_id"
    - "freshness_age"
    - "canonical_write_verification"
  never_record:
    - "source_payload"
    - "packet_payload_copy"
    - "raw_content"
    - "credentials"
    - "private_links"
    - "vault_excerpt"
  alerts:
    - "missed_schedule"
    - "retry_exhausted"
    - "packet_quarantined"
    - "required_input_stale"
    - "brief_blocked"
    - "unexpected_volume_change"
    - "permission_expansion_attempt"

rollout:
  current_stage: "schema_only"
  allowed_stages:
    - "schema_only"
    - "shadow"
    - "compare"
    - "canary"
    - "active"
  expand_one_source_at_a_time: true
  human_review_required_through_canary: true

rollback:
  disable_schedules_first: true
  revoke_scout_credentials_on_policy_breach: true
  stop_packet_promotion: true
  preserve_immutable_packets_and_briefs: true
  restore_previous_config_and_schema: true
  resume_in_shadow_mode: true
  autonomous_vault_rollback_allowed: false
